title: Allstate Insurance Co. v. Hague
lead: A Wisconsin accident led a widow to seek Minnesota’s more favorable insurance-stacking rule; five Justices allowed that choice of law, but they did not agree on a single constitutional explanation.

actors.name: Ralph Hague
actors.role: Wisconsin resident commuting to Minnesota work and deceased insured

actors.name: Mrs. Hague
actors.role: Widow, estate representative, and plaintiff seeking combined coverage

proceedings: Minnesota district court granted coverage declaration on summary judgment; Minnesota Supreme Court affirmed; U.S. Supreme Court affirmed 5–3, with Stevens separately concurring and Stewart not participating.
limits: Personal jurisdiction was undisputed. Constitutional permission to choose Minnesota law did not endorse its conflicts method or compel that choice. The Court did not award $45,000 in damages. A post-occurrence move alone was not held sufficient.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The insured lived in Wisconsin but worked across the state line
sections.cue: Establish the policy, accident, and later move in the right order.
paragraphs: Ralph Hague lived with his wife in Hager City, Wisconsin, about one and one-half miles from Red Wing, Minnesota. For fifteen years he worked in Red Wing and commuted daily. He died from injuries sustained as a motorcycle passenger in Pierce County, Wisconsin. Both operators were Wisconsin residents without valid insurance. The accident occurred neither in Minnesota nor during Hague’s commute, and none of his three insured automobiles was involved.

Allstate nevertheless provided uninsured-motorist protection beyond occupancy of those cars. Hague paid separate premiums, including uninsured-motorist premiums, for $15,000 coverage on each automobile. His widow sought to stack those amounts to obtain $45,000 coverage; Allstate urged Wisconsin law, which the Minnesota courts understood to prohibit stacking.

After the accident and before suing, Mrs. Hague moved to Red Wing and became the estate’s personal representative in Minnesota. The first move’s precise date was not in the record. Proceedings began May 28, 1976; she remarried a Minnesota resident June 19 and later moved to Savage. The plurality understood the stipulated circumstances as bona fide residence rather than a litigation-driven move.

sections.title: Minnesota chose its stacking rule and the Supreme Court reviewed only constitutional limits
sections.cue: Distinguish coverage choice from jurisdiction and damages.
paragraphs: The Minnesota district court applied forum law and granted Mrs. Hague summary judgment. Its supreme court affirmed using Professor Leflar’s considerations of predictability, interstate order, judicial simplification, forum interests, and the better rule of law. It emphasized Minnesota’s stacking rule and, on rehearing, mobile automobiles and insurance risks.

The U.S. Supreme Court reviewed whether that choice violated due process or full faith and credit. Personal jurisdiction over Allstate was unquestioned and analytically separate. The Court did not select a preferred conflicts method, decide the asserted false-conflict question, or award the requested coverage as damages.

sections.title: Brennan evaluated Minnesota’s contacts collectively
sections.cue: Introduce the precedents and the resulting state interests.
paragraphs: Justice Brennan, joined by White, Marshall, and Blackmun, required a significant contact or aggregation creating state interests sufficient to make selection neither arbitrary nor fundamentally unfair. More than one state’s law could constitutionally govern; the forum did not have to show its interests exceeded another’s.

He contrasted Dick, involving nominal Texas residence without meaningful connection to a Mexican insurance transaction, and Yates, involving a widow’s post-death move without other significant forum ties. Alaska Packers, Cardillo, and Clay II illustrated sufficient contacts despite an out-of-state injury or original policy. Recognition of judgments and records raised different questions from choice of governing law.

Three connections together supported Minnesota. Hague belonged to its workforce and regularly used its facilities and protections; Minnesota had interests in employee welfare, effects on employers, and vindication of an employee’s estate. A noncommuting Wisconsin accident did not erase every employment connection.

Allstate also did business in Minnesota, knew its insurance law, and had issued continental coverage without a Wisconsin choice clause. Combined with the Minnesota worker and resident representative, that presence weakened unfair-surprise claims and supplied a regulatory connection. Finally, Mrs. Hague’s bona fide residence and appointment supported a compensatory interest. The plurality did not permit unilateral law selection simply by moving; it expressly reserved whether the first two contacts, separately or together, would suffice without the third.

sections.title: Stevens separated sovereignty from fairness and rejected some plurality contacts
sections.cue: Explain why his fifth vote did not adopt Brennan’s reasoning.
paragraphs: Justice Stevens thought Minnesota’s choice unsound under ordinary conflicts principles but constitutionally permissible. Full faith and credit protected state sovereignty and national unity; due process protected litigants against arbitrariness or fundamental unfairness. Allstate had shown no unjustified infringement of Wisconsin’s legitimate interests. The policy anticipated travel and expressed no exclusive Wisconsin understanding on stacking.

Forum familiarity and efficient administration supported a presumption of rationality, but could not excuse fundamental unfairness. Here stacking was common, fit separate premiums, operated without discrimination, and contradicted no express policy provision. Nationwide coverage and Allstate’s local business made another state’s law foreseeable. Contract terms could inform expectations without invariably controlling them.

Stevens regarded the widow’s unexpected later move as irrelevant to earlier contracting expectations and Hague’s employment as adding nothing independently to this fairness analysis. Commuting at most reinforced the expectation already supplied by broad coverage. His concurrence rested on no demonstrated sovereignty violation or constitutional unfairness, not approval of the plurality’s use of those contacts. Federal review did not authorize a general federal conflicts rule.

sections.title: Powell found insufficient connection to the particular stacking policy
sections.cue: Close with the dissent’s actual objection and the vote.
paragraphs: Justice Powell, joined by Chief Justice Burger and Justice Rehnquist, accepted much of the plurality’s general formulation. He expressly agreed that no reasonable expectation was frustrated: national coverage and proximity to Minnesota made its law foreseeable. His objection was therefore not a finding of surprise.

He required contacts connected to the substantive policy being applied. The widow’s later residence did not relate the insurance claim to Minnesota when it arose. Allstate’s fifty-state business could not authorize every state to regulate unrelated contracts. Employment did not connect this private Wisconsin accident or benefit amount to Minnesota employment policy, and commuting and workplace could not simply be double-counted. A physical-contact tally was no substitute for that policy connection.

On January 13, 1981, the Court affirmed five to three. Stevens supplied the fifth judgment vote without joining Brennan, and Justice Stewart did not participate. Minnesota’s coverage ruling stood as constitutionally allowed, not constitutionally required.
